doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Designing the syllabus: expository materials and fairness
summary: The first semesters assess students with orchestra melodies and keyed material; everyone gets the same course so no one is treated differently.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yes in a sense. You know first of all a responsibility of a trumpet teacher, if you’re going to study with a trumpet teacher you have to learn how to play the trumpet. And a lot of students come to college and they have deficiencies. So the first two semesters of my syllabus are more or less expository. So everything is set up by keys and by like styles of music. Like I had one book that was called In the Singing Style. And what it was, was orchestra melodies, everything from a church hymn to a, you know, some kind of a part of some piece that a trumpet would play in an orchestra or something like that. So this way I could see, you know assess the depth of the knowledge of students in music. Then I would have the technical — we would start out with freshmen, everybody, it didn’t matter if they were virtuosic, all freshmen did the same course because you know what the academic ombudsman is, don’t you?
I’m going to let you tell me.

Well in most liberal arts colleges they usually don’t have one but I taught in Centres so I know that they don’t really have them. They have an academic counsel or something you know. But at State universities you know you have to treat everybody equally meaning from the standpoint of the coursework. You can’t say, “Oh, well Monk you know you’re not a very good reader so I’m going to give you this real easy thing to do and then at the end of the semester you can write a one-page summary of what we did this semester, and that’s all you need to do because you’re not as proficient” as this other person. Then this

other young person comes in, maybe the class is philosophy. “Well your mom and dad were both philosophers and they wrote books and things, so you have to read War and Peace and you have to tell me all the levels that this book is written on.” And then the guy that does the War and Peace gets a B, and guy that does the easy assignments because they just had no contact with music gets an A. You see that’s not fair. Just because that person is able you cannot treat them differently. So I wanted to make sure — and then also you find a lot of holes in that person that everybody thinks plays really well and that’s my job. My job is to bring everybody up to a certain standard. That’s what a course does. You have to learn as an applied teacher or any teacher in college you have to learn how to use their system to make what you need to happen happen. And over by you know like some people will turn in a syllabus that will say, “Fresh veneer, fundamentals.” What’s that? I mean that’s nothing. That’s say like, “Let’s eat.” You know what I mean? That’s fine but I mean I guess it’s effective but for that one situation — but I would say, “Let’s go to my favorite French restaurant. They have crepes. Crepes are this wonderful thing that you put stuff inside or on top of.” You see what I mean? You have to create depth if you are going to do something extraordinary.
